title: Verified Cool-Night Rooms for Heat-Stressed Europe
one_liner: Cheap in-room sensors prove a hotel room stays below about 26C at night, sold as a certificate, a refund guarantee and a machine-readable rating for booking agents.
customer: Hotels, B&Bs and STR operators in Greece, Italy, Spain, Croatia, Portugal and Turkey, with OTAs, agent builders and insurers as secondary buyers.
problem: Summer heat makes 'air-conditioned' meaningless, since old units, weak cooling and poor insulation leave rooms hot at night. Nobody measures indoor night temperature, so complaints turn into refund disputes. Rerouted demand into Turkey and Southern Europe, and a focus on 'value for money', make heat a rising complaint.
solution: Fit a USD 10-15 wireless sensor per room in about 10 minutes. It logs a nightly indoor temperature curve, and we issue a 'Cool Night verified' certificate showing the share of nights below the threshold, with a public verification page and JSON feed for AI agents and metasearch. Hotels also get a dashboard to find and fix problem rooms, and can add a hotel-funded heat refund guarantee.
why_now: Repeated European heatwaves, cheap connected sensors, and AI booking assistants that need structured, verifiable attributes because star ratings and 'AC yes/no' are uninformative. Booking's commoditisation of listings makes measured differentiation valuable to independents.
revenue_model: EUR 6-9 per room per month, a EUR 150 install kit, an annual certification fee, and data licensing to platforms.
non_obvious_insight: Comfort is the one hotel attribute that is physically measurable yet almost never measured. In a world of agent-driven booking, a verified physical attribute becomes a ranking signal.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 hotels in Athens, Crete, Sicily and Puglia using off-the-shelf sensors. Offer a free 30-day 'truth test' and publish an anonymised heat report for press. Convert 10 to paid subscriptions.

title: Liquidity for Managers of Overheld PE Companies
one_liner: Give executives in stuck PE portfolio companies a way to cash out part of their vested equity through third-party buyers, so sponsors can fix management retention without diluting the fund or forcing an exit.
customer: Lower-middle-market PE sponsors and independent sponsors holding 2019-2021 vintage platforms. They pay for the diagnostic. Portfolio-company CEOs, CFOs and operators hold vested profits interests or options. Family offices and secondary funds supply the capital that buys management equity.
problem: Hold periods have stretched to roughly seven years. Management teams are fatigued and their incentive plans have lost value, which raises the risk they leave. The fund cannot exit (LPs tolerate little markdown), and topping up the management incentive plan (MIP) dilutes the sponsor's remaining upside.
solution: (1) A 'MIP Health Check': a waterfall model built from the operating agreement showing each manager's equity value under three exit dates and prices, with a retention-risk score. (2) A 'management tender desk': arrange third-party purchase of 10-25% of a manager's vested units at a negotiated discount, with sponsor consent and rights of first refusal, funded by a syndicate of family offices and secondary funds. (3) A cost and dilution comparison against a traditional MIP reload. Structured through a registered broker-dealer partner and securities counsel.
why_now: Bain's 2026 midyear report says most buyout assets were acquired in 2021 or earlier, the implied capital cycle is about seven years, and roughly one in five LPs are cutting buyout allocations. Bain's year-end outlook counts 32,000 unrealized companies worth $3.8T and says 40% of portfolio companies are held over 5 years, versus 29% in 2019. Fund-level returns flatten after year eight, so the pressure to retain operators through the extended hold is acute.
revenue_model: $5-10K per MIP Health Check billed to the sponsor. 1.5-3% placement fee on tender volume, paid by buyers. Later, SaaS for waterfall tracking at $1-3K/month per fund.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is human capital inside assets that cannot be sold, and the only retention lever that costs the fund nothing in dilution is third-party liquidity for managers. Bain's midyear report says: 'Stretched holding periods have fatigued management teams and depleted incentive plan value, complicating mid-hold value-creation refreshes,' and that more than half of LPs cap tolerated markdowns on full exits at 5%, which pushes GPs to hold underperformers longer (https://www.bain.com/insights/private-equity-midyear-report-2026/). 'Stretched holds' and '12 is the new 5' EBITDA growth targets (https://www.bain.com/insights/welcome-to-a-new-era-global-private-equity-report-2026/) mean operators are being asked to deliver more for longer. Employee tender offers are routine in venture-backed startups but are, by my inference, rare for PE-backed profits interests, so this looks like an open niche. That is an inference from the sources, not something they state. Regulatory structure is the main risk.
first_30_days: Build a profits-interest waterfall calculator from a standard operating-agreement template. Retain securities and tax counsel for a scoping memo and line up a registered broker-dealer partner. Offer free Health Checks to 15 independent sponsors and lower-mid-market GPs with 2019-2021 vintage assets, reached through ACG, Searchfunder and direct outreach. Then sign 2-3 paid checks at $5K and use the results to pitch one family office to fund a first tender.

title: Loss Draft Desk for Storm Contractors
one_liner: Software and concierge service that gets contractors and homeowners through the mortgage servicer's loss-draft process, then advances cash against approved draws.
customer: Storm-restoration general contractors, roofers and owner-builders working on mortgage-encumbered repairs and rebuilds, starting with the Palisades and Eaton rebuild wave and Gulf Coast stragglers. Later, homeowners and the servicers' own vendor teams.
problem: The carrier pays, but the money is not free: the check names the mortgagee, and the servicer's loss-draft department decides whether to release it in one lump sum or in staged draws tied to inspections. Each servicer has its own packet (contractor W-9, license, signed contract, lien waivers, before/after photos, inspection scheduling) and its own cadence. Contractors carry 60-120 days of working capital risk, homeowners cannot start work, and adjusters take the blame for a delay that comes after the estimate is done.
solution: A draw-management platform: it reads the carrier's payment letter and the servicer's requirements, auto-builds and submits the servicer-specific packet, schedules and preps for inspections (checklist plus timestamped photo capture), chases the servicer, and shows the contractor and homeowner a live 'money timeline.' Phase two adds a draw advance: after the servicer approves a draw schedule, the platform advances 80-90% of the next draw in days, underwritten on proprietary servicer-by-servicer release data.
why_now: Florida's AOB ban (for policies since 2023) means contractors cannot be paid directly by carriers, so they must wait on homeowners and servicers. The LA fire rebuild in 2026-27 involves thousands of large, mortgage-encumbered claims and long draw schedules. Materials costs remain volatile, which squeezes contractor cash. Regulatory rules and GSE guidelines push servicers to release funds promptly after approving a repair plan but leave the mechanics unstandardized, creating a compliance-flavored process that software can systematize.
revenue_model: Flat $295-$495 per job, or 0.5-1% of funds released. Draw advances at 2-3% of advance amount plus a 30-60 day fee, funded by a warehouse credit line. Later, per-file fees from servicers who want clean packets and fewer complaint escalations.
non_obvious_insight: The real payment terms in disaster repair are the servicer's draw curve, not the insurance company's payment speed, and nobody publishes it. Whoever logs, servicer by servicer, days-to-first-draw, inspection pass rates and packet rejection reasons owns the underwriting data for the only safe lending against insurance proceeds.
first_30_days: Sign up 5 mid-size LA fire rebuild contractors and 5 Gulf Coast roofers and offer to run their next 3 jobs through the loss-draft process as a done-for-you service at $295 per job. Log every servicer requirement in a shared spreadsheet, then turn it into a rules engine. Interview 3 former loss-draft department employees for packet-rejection patterns. Start collecting draw-timeline data, which becomes the moat and the basis for a later advance product.

title: Tell Us Once: US Death-Event Switchboard
one_liner: Verify an executor once, then let agents notify and close dozens of institutions for you, building toward a reusable 'authority to act' credential the institutions accept.
customer: Executors and surviving families pay, with distribution through funeral homes, estate attorneys and employers or insurers. Institutions later pay per verified case.
problem: US executors call dozens of banks, card issuers, utilities and subscription companies, each demanding its own certified death certificate, letters and forms. The deceased's identity is exposed to fraud. The UK has 'Tell Us Once', the US has nothing, and the brief finds no dominant software owner of the estate close-out workflow.
solution: The executor uploads the death certificate, ID and letters. The system verifies them once, then voice and browser agents run institution-specific playbooks: credit bureau alerts, identity locks, marketing suppression, subscription and utility cancellations or transfers, date-of-death balance requests and claim forms. A status board tracks every account, and human ops handle exceptions. Over time it issues a verified executor credential institutions accept by API.
why_now: Voice agents that navigate phone trees and hold queues, and browser agents that complete web forms, reached usable reliability in 2025-26. Digital ID wallets are spreading. Insurer and employer channels such as Empathy (50M+ covered policyholders) show buyers for bereavement services, but Empathy is not a close-out execution layer.
revenue_model: $199-$399 flat per estate ($99 wholesale to funeral homes), $10-$40 per verified case from institutions, and insurer or employer benefit contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is repeated verification, not the work itself. A reusable, verified authority credential collapses 60 identical fights into one and gives institutions a fraud-reduction reason to cooperate.
first_30_days: Build playbooks for the top 30 institutions (big banks, card issuers, brokers, telecoms, streaming, credit bureaus). Sell 25 human-in-the-loop cases through 5 funeral homes at $149. Record each institution's requirements to build the data moat.

title: Walker Brain: Clip-On Sensor for Rollators
one_liner: A $60 clip-on pod that turns any walker or rollator into a fall alarm, night-light and gait-speed monitor, so there is no wearable to forget.
customer: Home-care agencies and PACE programs (buying for clients), DME suppliers, Medicare Advantage and ACO care teams, and adult children buying directly.
problem: Pendant alarms fail because many seniors won't wear them or press them. People who use walkers are among the highest fall-risk group, yet smart-walker work is mostly academic prototypes. Gait speed predicts decline and hospitalization but is measured in a clinic once a year, if at all.
solution: A clamp-on pod with an IMU, LTE-M connectivity, a small LED light strip, tip and fall detection and grip sensing. It detects when the walker is actually being used versus left by the bed at night, which is itself a leading risk signal. It auto-alerts on tipping and sends a weekly gait report and decline flags to family and the care team. Battery lasts months and the senior needs no app.
why_now: Low-power LTE-M and IMU chips are cheap. Medicare Advantage plans are measured on fall-risk management, and home-care agencies are looking for differentiation. The DME channel has not changed in decades, and the walker sensor category is still mostly prototypes.
revenue_model: Hardware $59-79, family subscription $8-12/month. B2B: about $6 per pod per month for agencies, or a per-member-per-month fee for plan pilots.
non_obvious_insight: Don't ask an 80-year-old to adopt a new device. Instrument the one object they can't give up and that is with them exactly when risk peaks. 'Walker left behind at night' is a signal no wearable can capture.
first_30_days: Prototype with off-the-shelf LTE-M dev boards and a 3D-printed clamp. Place 30 pods on walkers with 3 home-care agencies as free trials. Measure alerts and gait trends. Aim to convert 2 agencies to 100-unit pilots, and talk to outpatient physical therapists about a small validation study.

title: Peak-Season Exchange for Idle Warehouse Robot Hours
one_liner: A marketplace and price index that moves idle AMRs and robots-as-a-service capacity between 3PLs and retailers to cover seasonal peaks, priced per robot-hour.
customer: Mid-size 3PLs and retailers needing Q4 peak capacity, and owners of idle fleets (integrators, RaaS providers, seasonal retailers, lenders holding repossessed units). Lenders and investors buy the index.
problem: Peaks force 3PLs into premium temp labor, while fleets sized for average load sit idle for half the year at seasonal operators. There is no market price for a robot-hour, so lenders cannot value the assets either.
solution: Standardize robot-hour listings (AMR class, payload, WMS integration) with a 48-hour commissioning kit (mapping, WMS connector) and escrowed insurance. Seed supply from idle demo pools and seasonal owners, and publish a weekly Robot Rate Index by class and region. Add forward contracts for peak later.
why_now: Robot pricing is becoming public and recurring (Figure's planned $600 a month lease, 1X at $499 a month, Agility's $300M+ order), and buyers want outcome pricing and 48-hour product-mix changes. Peak season 2026 is starting now, so the first rentals can be tested against real labor premiums.
revenue_model: 12-18% take rate on rentals, a commissioning fee per deployment, and $10-30k a year for index and benchmark subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Robots are sold as capex but bought as capacity. Once tens of thousands of units exist, capacity will trade like trailers and rail cars, and whoever runs the exchange sets the price benchmark (DAT, Drewry) and owns residual-value data.
first_30_days: Source about 50 idle AMRs from 2 integrators' demo pools and 2 seasonal retailers. Sell 3 emergency Q4 peak rentals to 3PLs paying temp-labor premiums, and publish Robot Rate Index v0 from about 40 collected quotes.

title: Pre-Permitted Gateway Campuses for Satellite Constellations
one_liner: A real-estate developer for multi-tenant satellite gateway sites with power, fiber, interference studies and landing-right support.
customer: Constellation operators (broadband, direct-to-cell, EO downlink) that need dozens of gateways in many countries, and ground-station-as-a-service providers.
problem: Every constellation needs gateways that are radio-quiet, low in rain fade, and connected to fiber and power. Zoning, community opposition and national landing rights make site acquisition slow, and launching more satellites does not help if gateways are the bottleneck. AST is launch-constrained now, but ground capacity is next.
solution: Option, entitle and pre-permit 'gateway campuses' in strategic regions, then lease antenna pads on 10-15 year terms. Include interference and rain-fade studies, fiber and power, and local licensing help. Start in the Caribbean, Latin America and Africa, where landing rights and site scarcity bind hardest.
why_now: Launch capacity is exploding, so the bottleneck shifts to the ground. Spectrum is now owned by operators with big plans (SpaceX, AT&T, AST). Direct-to-cell needs many gateways to reach many carriers.
revenue_model: Pad leases $8-25k per month per antenna. Development fee on entitlement assignment. Long-term power and fiber pass-through margin.
non_obvious_insight: Operators over-invest in satellites and under-invest in the boring ground sites that gate capacity. Zoning boards, not rockets, may be the binding constraint.
first_30_days: Use GIS to shortlist 30 parcels near fiber and power across five regions. Take low-cost options on five. Get LOIs from two gateway-hungry operators or teleport providers before spending on entitlements.

title: Cube Receipt: Win LTL Reclass and Reweigh Disputes
one_liner: A 45-second phone-based dimension-and-weight capture at the shipper's dock produces a timestamped, tamper-evident record attached to the BOL, then used to contest LTL carrier reclass and reweigh charges on contingency.
customer: Small and mid-size B2B shippers with $50K-$2M in annual LTL spend (furniture and home-goods makers, craft food and beverage, DTC brands shipping pallets, HVAC and parts distributors), plus small brokers who arrange LTL and absorb the adjustments when customers refuse to pay.
problem: The NMFC update on July 19, 2025 moved a large number of item numbers to density-based classification. Carriers reweigh and re-dimension freight at terminals with automated dimensioners and bill the corrected class, commonly a $30-$75 fee plus a 20-50% rate uplift. The shipper has no evidence of what actually left the dock, so the carrier's inspection is judge and jury. Most shippers just pay, and brokers who booked the load eat a share when the customer will not.
solution: A mobile app (iPhone LiDAR or camera) walks the packer through a pallet capture: dimensions with a reference marker, weight from a scale photo or entry, density and class check, wrap-bulge and overhang warnings, then hash and timestamp. It generates a QR sticker and a PDF appended to the BOL. When an adjustment invoice arrives (ingested from carrier emails or the freight audit feed), it auto-files the dispute with the evidence, tracks the carrier response, and takes a share of money recovered. It also flags pre-shipment problems, such as stretch-wrap bulge and pallet lip that inflate carrier-measured cube.
why_now: The July 2025 NMFC density shift is still generating adjustment invoices in 2026, and shippers are still learning the new classes. Phone LiDAR is ubiquitous, and carrier dimensioners are now the default at terminals, which makes source-side evidence the missing counterweight.
revenue_model: 25-30% of recovered adjustment charges (contingency), or $99-$299/month per dock. White-label to brokers at about $0.75 per shipment.
non_obvious_insight: Reclass is an evidence-asymmetry game, not a classification problem. The carrier's dimensioner records at the terminal and the shipper has nothing from the source. Terminal cube often includes bulging wrap and the pallet lip. A record made at tender time beats an after-the-fact photo inside the dispute window. Brokers see this daily in adjustment invoices but treat it as a cost of doing business rather than a product.
first_30_days: Approach 10 brokers who place LTL for small shippers. Each has adjustment invoices sitting in AR. Take six months of them, run manual disputes on contingency using whatever photos the shippers have, and log win rates by carrier. Build a no-code capture form (photo checklist plus timestamp) and put it on 3 shippers' docks. Use the win-rate data to sell the app.

title: Drone Incident Desk for Cities and Venues
one_liner: Detection-to-handoff service that turns a drone sighting into a documented, legally routed federal referral for local agencies that cannot legally jam anything.
customer: City emergency management and police departments, stadium and arena operators, and event promoters at major events. Dallas has $10M set aside, and FEMA has a $500M counter-UAS grant program.
problem: Insiders see counter-drone as a radar and jammer hardware sale. Local police mostly lack legal authority to mitigate, and protocols with FBI and DHS are unclear. FBI and DHS seized more than 700 drones near one stadium during the World Cup. Cities are buying sensors with no playbook for what to do next.
solution: Vendor-neutral software plus a 24/7 human desk. It ingests alerts from whatever sensors a venue owns (RF, Remote ID, radar) and classifies them. It geolocates the pilot, routes the incident to the correct federal or state authority, and packages a chain-of-custody evidence file. Includes tabletop drills and after-action reports.
why_now: The World Cup exposed the gap. FEMA counter-UAS grant money is arriving at localities. Future mega-events raise urgency, and Remote ID data is now broadly available.
revenue_model: Annual subscription per venue or city ($40-150K), event-surge packages, and drill or training fees. It also helps grant applicants justify sensor purchases.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is purchasing liability cover and a working relationship with federal agencies, not detection accuracy. Sensors will commoditize, but the handoff protocol and evidence trail will not.
first_30_days: Interview 10 emergency managers and venue security directors in World Cup host cities. Build the desk on a shared inbox plus a case-management tool. Offer a free tabletop exercise to 3 venues and convert one to a paid pilot.

title: Notarized Sky: Satellite Image Authenticity Desk
one_liner: A verification desk that tells insurers, traders and newsrooms whether a 'satellite photo' is real, by corroborating it against independent archives and issuing a signed chain-of-custody attestation.
customer: Marine war-risk and political-violence underwriters and brokers in the London market, commodity and energy trading desks, and verification desks at wire services and OSINT outlets. Second wave: parametric insurers whose triggers depend on Earth-observation data, and arbitration or sanctions law firms.
problem: Generative tools can now fabricate or subtly edit overhead imagery, and viral 'satellite photos' of strikes, burning tankers or troop moves circulate in every conflict, moving prices and claims. Buyers assume satellites are physics-grade truth, but the last mile is a JPEG on social media and vendors sell pixels, not provenance. With the Strait of Hormuz reportedly closed since March 2026, war-risk claims and rumor-driven price moves are large.
solution: (1) Rapid 'witness triangulation': check the claimed place and time against open archives (Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2, Landsat) and quick commercial archive pulls (optical and SAR), plus sun-angle and shadow geometry, cloud and terrain consistency, and vessel positions versus AIS and RF logs. (2) Forensics for synthetic or edited artifacts and C2PA/EXIF provenance. (3) A signed, hash-timestamped corroboration report usable in claims files and disputes. (4) For imagery buyers, verify delivered files against provider manifests.
why_now: Hormuz disruption created a wave of unverifiable incident claims. EU AI Act Article 50(2) synthetic-content marking applies from 2 Dec 2026 for systems already on the market, raising attention on provenance. Commodity EO and SAR are cheap and frequent (Planet targets up to 10 revisits a day), but no cross-vendor 'signed pixels' standard exists.
revenue_model: $2.5-8K per rapid verification report (24-hour SLA) and $8-20K per month retainers for underwriters and desks. Later, metered API access for parametric insurers.
non_obvious_insight: Detection accuracy is not the product; corroboration is. Government-held archives cannot be retroactively edited by an attacker, and SAR sees through cloud and is not something a text-to-image model can fake convincingly. A tiny team can be an independent witness cheaply. What buyers actually pay for is a defensible attestation, a SOC report for pixels, that survives a claims dispute.
first_30_days: Publish teardowns of 3 viral fake or misattributed satellite images from 2025-26 conflicts, each with reproducible multi-source refutations. Send them to 25 marine war-risk brokers and 15 newsroom verification desks. Sell 3 rapid-verification pilots at $2.5K each and convert one underwriter to a retainer.

title: Reusable Trust Passport for Bio-AI Access
one_liner: One neutral, portable verification that a biotech or academic lab is legitimate, bound to that lab's agent keys, so frontier AI vendors and DNA/reagent suppliers can accept its agent-placed orders without repeating the diligence.
customer: Small and mid-size biotechs, academic labs and CROs that need relaxed AI safeguards and want agents to order DNA, oligos and reagents. Secondary payers are AI vendors and suppliers who pay per verified check.
problem: On September 17, 2026 Anthropic launched its Life Sciences Verification Program (credential, security and ethics-oversight review, 30-day data retention) and expected hundreds of organizations in week one. Other AI providers, DNA synthesis vendors and cloud labs will each build their own version. Small labs lack SOC 2-style security paperwork, organized IBC documentation or an ethics-oversight file, so they queue or get denied. Machine identities already outnumber humans about 109 to 1 and there is no shared 'know your agent' standard for bio orders.
solution: A one-time dossier (organization identity, IBC/IACUC registration, named biosafety officer, lightweight security review, data-handling policy) issued as a verifiable credential tied to the lab's agent keys. AI vendors and suppliers accept it for access tiers and agent-placed orders, and the credential is continuously monitored and revoked if an IBC approval lapses. Include a readiness checklist and concierge help to complete the paperwork.
why_now: Verification programs started in September 2026, creating an immediate backlog and duplicative-paperwork problem. Agent-order volume is growing, and synthesis-screening rules and frontier-lab safeguards are tightening at the same time.
revenue_model: Flat verification fee ($1.5-5K one-time plus annual renewal), per-check fees from vendors and AI providers, and an enterprise tier for CRO networks and shared core facilities.
non_obvious_insight: Frontier labs cannot be each other's trust anchor, which is why an accredited third-party reviewer that several of them accept is valuable. This is the Vanta/Plaid pattern applied to bio access, and the first concierge revenue comes from the backlog, before any network effect exists.
first_30_days: Build the 'verification readiness' checklist and offer a $2.5K flat concierge service to the first 20 labs that applied. Talk to 3 mid-tier DNA/oligo vendors and 2 cloud labs about accepting your dossier for agent orders. Publish an open template so vendors see you as the standards-setter, then charge for review and monitoring.

title: Tele-Clearance for Sheriffs' Booking Desks
one_liner: A night-shift nurse-and-NP screening service that lets a rural deputy clear an arrestee for booking from the jail, without spending four hours in the ER while the county goes unpatrolled.
customer: County sheriffs and county commissioners, funded through county risk pools and insurers (for example state association-of-counties liability pools) that pay for jail deaths and lawsuits. Paid per county per month.
problem: Rural jails often have no on-site medical staff, so jail policy requires a hospital 'medical clearance' for any arrestee who is intoxicated, injured or says his chest hurts. At 2am the deputy brings the person to the ER and sits with him for 3-5 hours, sometimes the county's only deputy on duty. The county pays a $2,000-4,000 ER bill and has nobody patrolling. The ER meanwhile holds a bed and a nurse for someone with nothing acutely wrong except being drunk. When clearance is skipped, the risk is a death in custody from alcohol or opioid withdrawal, a head injury or diabetic crisis, which is a lawsuit.
solution: A booking-desk kit (vitals, pulse oximeter, glucometer, breathalyzer, tablet) plus 24/7 on-demand video screening by an RN and NP working from home, using a physician-signed clearance protocol built from ACEP's published best-practice guidance for patients in custody. Dispositions are 'fit for booking with monitoring plan', 'needs ER now', or 're-check in 2 hours'. The service also creates a documented withdrawal-watch checklist, such as sobriety and CIWA-style monitoring, which jails need for liability reasons. The report is time-stamped and defensible.
why_now: Rural hospital and ER closures are lengthening transport times. Prison Policy Initiative reported in October 2025 that about half of incarcerated people are held in rural jails and prisons that risk losing hospital access. Medicaid cuts and the pressure on county budgets are also forcing sheriffs to look for cheaper options, and some already release people on 'medical bond' to avoid ER bills. Telehealth billing and licensure flexibility, together with the Nurse Licensure Compact, make cross-state night staffing workable.
revenue_model: $2,000-3,500 per county per month, including up to about 40 screens. Additional screens are $85 each. Roughly 12 counties would support a team of 6 part-time clinicians. Later, sell an outcome dashboard called 'deputy hours returned to patrol', which is the number commissioners and risk-pool underwriters will care about most.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone frames the problem as ER wait time or inmate healthcare. From inside the ER, the real cost is the deputy who is stuck with us. In a county with one or two deputies on at night, an ER trip is a public safety hole, and the buyer will pay to close it. Also, most 'medical clearances' are defensive medicine that a good screen would make unnecessary. Big correctional health vendors (Wellpath, NaphCare) sell staffing for large jails and are not built for a 12-bed jail on a county road.
first_30_days: Write the clearance protocol with a supervising physician from a rural ER and get it reviewed by one county attorney. Choose one sheriff the founder already knows from ER encounters. Run a paid pilot at $1,500 for 60 days and count deputy hours saved and ER trips avoided. Then pitch the state's county risk pool and sheriffs' association with the numbers.

title: Second-Life Desal Membranes for Farms and Towns
one_liner: Buy retired reverse-osmosis elements from big desal plants, test and recondition them, and sell them with a performance guarantee to farms, greenhouses and small systems.
customer: Brackish-water growers and greenhouse operators (Arizona, Texas, Imperial and Yuma areas), oilfield produced-water treaters, and small utilities, starting non-potable. Sellers of used elements are large plants. Buyers pay per element.
problem: Large plants replace a slice of their elements every year, and a commonly cited literature figure puts discarded RO membranes at over ten thousand tonnes annually. Small brackish and farm users pay $600-1,200 per new element and face lead times. Desal is spreading as costs fall (about $0.50/m3 typical, with a reported $0.28/m3 waste-heat plant in China that is not fully verified), and Cyprus approved an 85M euro mobile unit in April 2026.
solution: Acquire retired elements, then test flux, rejection and pressure drop. Clean and sort by remaining performance. Sell 'certified reconditioned' elements with a guarantee to non-potable users. Offer plants a take-back service (they avoid disposal cost and gain a circularity claim). Add a membrane-health monitoring subscription and, later, downcycle to nanofiltration and ultrafiltration. Potable use needs NSF certification, so leave it for later.
why_now: The desal fleet is growing worldwide, farms need cheap brackish-water treatment as river cuts arrive, and the aftermarket is untouched because of warranty fear.
revenue_model: $150-450 per reconditioned element, take-back fees from plants, and monitoring subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Membranes are a consumable like tires, in a growing market where everyone innovates on new chemistry and nobody tests the aftermarket. An independent test standard plus a performance guarantee turns a landfill cost into low-cost supply.
first_30_days: Contact five brackish and seawater plant operators and used-element brokers. Buy 200 used elements. Rent test-rig time from a university lab or build a $30-60k rig. Sell five trial sets to greenhouse or ag operators in Arizona or Texas.

title: Physical-Properties Index for Every SKU
one_liner: A shared 'Gracenote for grasping': weight, center of mass, deformability, best grip points and packaging traits for millions of SKUs, sold to pick-robot makers and brands.
customer: Pick-and-pack robot vendors, 3PLs running robotic induction, CPG and retail brands (for robot-ready packaging certification), and humanoid developers.
problem: Picking robots fail on the long tail because they meet every SKU cold, and brands change packaging without notice. Amazon knows internally, but everyone else relearns per site.
solution: Fill the index from two sources: a scanning rig at partner 3PLs (3D scan, mass, center of mass, slip tests) and give-to-get contributions from robot fleets reporting grasp outcomes. Serve it by GTIN through an API with recommended grasp points and packing advice, and offer brands a 'Robot-Ready' grade that 3PLs reward with lower handling fees.
why_now: Robotic picking is now at scale (Amazon 1M+ robots, Symbotic $2.25B revenue, Maven-style mixed palletizing), and foundation models can use priors like these. A market of data buyers already exists.
revenue_model: API fees per lookup or per robot per month, $2-10k per SKU family for brand certification, and dataset licensing to model labs.
non_obvious_insight: Robots will not scale on smarter grasping alone. The world's goods need a machine-readable physical spec, and brands have a direct incentive because 3PLs and retailers will reward robot-ready packaging. A neutral index can become a standard the way GS1 barcodes did.
first_30_days: Build a $15k scanning rig at a friendly 3PL and scan the top 3,000 SKUs. Release a free tier, sign 2 pick-robot vendors as beta partners, and run one paid brand packaging audit.

title: Contingency-Fee Audit of OTA Markups and Payouts
one_liner: Mystery-shop every downstream reseller and reconcile every OTA payout, then take a share of the money and direct bookings recovered.
customer: Independent hotels of 20-200 rooms and small groups in Europe and the US paying 15-28% commissions.
problem: 51% of European hotels say OTAs sell below their loaded rate, up from 40% two years ago, and 26% do not know whether rates are passed on. Markups by Agoda, Citi, AA, Southwest and loyalty partners are invisible to rate-shopping tools. Hotels are paid after checkout, and commission, virtual-card fee and no-show errors go unchecked. In-house monitoring exists for chains (Radisson watches 1,600 properties), but independents have nothing.
solution: Combine automated and human shoppers that check rates across OTAs and reseller portals with screenshots per date, and reservation-level reconciliation of booked rate, commission, payout, card fees, cancellations and no-shows. Produce evidence packs to send to OTA account managers and a price-integrity dashboard that supports the case for direct booking.
why_now: Booking's payment service touched about 70% of its 2025 bookings, which concentrates the opacity. Google AI Overviews now reportedly show hotel prices and cut metasearch clicks, which pushes hotels to defend direct channels. Channel managers now expose reservation data.
revenue_model: 20-25% of recovered commission and no-show revenue, plus USD 99-299 per month for ongoing price-integrity monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: OTAs cannot audit themselves and hotels cannot see downstream markups, the same structural gap that made freight-bill and telecom-audit firms lucrative. The shopping evidence is the leverage in negotiations.
first_30_days: Offer 20 hotels a free 'leak report' covering 30 future dates, using human plus scripted shoppers. Convert the worst-leaking ones to contingency contracts, using hotel associations for introductions.

title: Resident Proof for Two-Tier Tourist Pricing
one_liner: A privacy-preserving QR proof of residence lets towns, museums and transit charge visitors more and locals less without building databases or discriminating by nationality.
customer: Municipalities and municipal attractions, ferries and parking in overrun towns of 5-100K people (Italy, Croatia, Spain, Japan), then private attractions and restaurants offering locals-first pricing.
problem: Insiders think dual pricing is a legal and PR minefield, useful only in niche places. It is spreading (reported moves include Rome's charge for non-resident visitors at the Trevi Fountain and resident-versus-visitor pricing at some Japanese castles). The real bottleneck is verification. Each site checks IDs by hand, builds a one-off app or discriminates crudely.
solution: Issue a wallet pass from the municipal residents' register, first over the town hall counter and later through national digital-ID wallets. It discloses only 'resident of X'. Gates and apps verify it offline, and the same pass unlocks locals-first booking windows and discounts. The town gets analytics on non-resident flows to tune fees.
why_now: Venice's flat fee reportedly did not reduce numbers, so cities are turning to differentiated pricing. EU member states must offer digital identity wallets by the end of 2026, which makes selective-disclosure credentials mainstream. Resident backlash is at its peak.
revenue_model: Municipal SaaS of EUR 10-30K per year, EUR 0.01-0.05 per verification, and an integration fee per attraction.
non_obvious_insight: Pricing policy is not the bottleneck; identity is. Whoever standardises the 'resident' claim owns the tollbooth for every future visitor-management rule, including resident-first windows, non-resident caps and local discounts.
first_30_days: Approach one town of 5-20K people that runs a municipal attraction, ferry or car park. Offer a free 90-day pilot where staff issue passes at the town hall and verify them with phone cameras. Use mayors' associations to find the pilot, and have a lawyer confirm the residency-based structure is proportionate.

title: Battery-Free Soil Tags Read by Drone
one_liner: Disposable soil moisture and salinity tags that need no battery and are read by drone flyover.
customer: Agronomy service providers, co-ops and specialty-crop growers with irrigated fields.
problem: Farmers face fertilizer and diesel volatility with no pricing power, yet soil data stays sparse because sensors cost too much and need batteries.
solution: Sub-$3 ambient-backscatter tags placed at planting and read from a drone or planter-mounted reader, starting with moisture and salinity and adding nitrate later.
why_now: Ambient-IoT chips scaled in 2025, and urea swinging from $400 to $850 to about $453/t makes precise input use valuable.
revenue_model: Per-tag fee plus a per-acre mapping and reading service.
non_obvious_insight: Soil sampling stays sparse because sensors are expensive. Making them disposable makes dense maps feasible.
first_30_days: Buy ambient-IoT development kits, prove drone readout at short range, and run a small field pilot on two farms.

title: Deepfake Shields for Mayors, Sold Through Risk Pools
one_liner: Long-tail likeness and voice protection for roughly 500,000 local elected officials, clerks and first responders who have no agency to police impersonation, sold as a loss-control service through municipal insurance risk pools and county election offices.
customer: State and regional municipal risk pools and cyber pools ($300-1,500 per member per year), county election offices ($500-2,000 each), and sheriffs' and police chiefs' associations.
problem: YouTube's likeness detection reached celebrities through CAA, UTA and WME in April 2026 with no path for anyone else, and voice clones need only seconds of audio (prior knowledge). Local officials are high-impact targets: a cloned 'mayor' telling finance staff to wire funds, fake curfew or polling-place notices, fake council videos. Local IT is thin (Dallas County is cutting 31 IT staff), federal election-security help to localities was scaled back in 2025 (prior knowledge), and the midterms are Nov 3, 2026.
solution: Enroll officials with consented voice and face references and monitor major platforms using existing detection APIs. Run a human takedown desk using platform impersonation policies and state deepfake statutes. Give finance staff call-back code-word protocols and quarterly voice-clone drills, and deliver evidence packs for insurers and police.
why_now: Midterm urgency, celebrity-only platform tools, and cheap high-quality voice cloning all arrive together. Pools face rising social-engineering claims (inference), and EU Article 50 plus platform enforcement raise expectations that impersonations get pulled quickly.
revenue_model: A per-member fee paid by the pool, per-incident takedown fees, drill fees, and premium credits negotiated with the pool.
non_obvious_insight: The 'agency' that long-tail people lack is the insurance pool. It already pays social-engineering claims, has member-services budgets, and can buy for a thousand towns in one sale. Framing the product as claims reduction rather than reputation management is what unlocks the budget.
first_30_days: Interview 5 pool loss-control managers and sell a $499 election-season kit to 20 county clerks. Run a free voice-clone drill for one pool's treasurers association to produce a claim-reduction case study.

title: Mother-Tongue Lifeline for Dementia Flashpoints
one_liner: On-demand live video calls where a dementia-trained speaker of the patient's first language and dialect coaches the English-speaking aide and calms the patient at bath, bedtime and exit-seeking moments.
customer: Home care agencies and PACE programs in immigrant-dense metros (NYC, LA, Miami, Chicago, Bay Area, Houston) with dementia clients whose aides do not share their language. Second: Medicaid managed long-term care and D-SNP plans. Third: families on a flat monthly plan.
problem: Bilingual and multilingual patients lose their second language as dementia advances and drift back to the language, dialect and idioms of their childhood. Agencies send whoever is available. The English-speaking aide cannot say the one calming phrase during the bath, so the bath fails, the patient panics, the aide gets hurt or quits, and the family blames the agency. Telephone interpretation lines translate literally, but a dementia patient's fragments and proverbs need to be validated, not translated. It is a communication problem, not an interpretation problem.
solution: A dedicated line, staffed on demand by trained bilingual retirees, nurses and teachers, covering the long tail: Yiddish, Haitian Creole, Toisanese, Cantonese, Polish, Russian, Uzbek, Punjabi, Tagalog, Greek, Armenian. A tablet or phone is propped where the patient can see it. The specialist speaks to the patient in dialect while coaching the aide in English in the earpiece: 'she's asking for her sister, say she is coming, then hum this song.' Sessions are 3-10 minutes at known flashpoints. Specialists are trained by aides in validation and redirection, not interpretation.
why_now: The post-war Soviet, Chinese, Caribbean and Southeast Asian immigrant cohorts who arrived in the 1960s-80s are now reaching moderate-to-severe dementia. Low-latency video is universal and cheap. AI companions such as KindredMind (voice clone of the caregiver, 12 languages, launched worldwide in May 2026) prove the demand, but they work best for mild cases and comfortable tech users. For moderate-to-severe dementia and live crises, the warm human voice in the right village dialect is the missing complement, and the agencies will pay per minute for it.
revenue_model: $1.25-1.75 per minute billed to agencies and plans, with 60-70 percent gross margin after specialist pay of about $0.45 per minute. Families get $129 per month for 20 sessions. Later, enterprise contracts with MLTC and D-SNP plans that cover the cost as a quality tool.
non_obvious_insight: Patients revert not just to a language but to a specific dialect and era, for example Toisanese, not Mandarin, and the idioms of 1955. A literal interpreter is useless because what calms is tone, a lullaby, a proverb and a familiar name. The buyer is not the family but the agency, which is desperate because language mismatch is why its aides quit its hardest cases. Nobody pays interpreters for companionship, so this talent pool of bilingual retirees is unmined and cheap.
first_30_days: Pick two languages with dense local demand, for example Toisanese or Cantonese in NYC and Haitian Creole in Miami. Recruit 10 bilingual retirees through churches, senior centers and community media. Train them in a one-page validation script. Run it on WhatsApp video with no software. Call 15 small agencies serving those communities and offer 30 free minutes per case. Sign the first three at $1.50 per minute with a $300 monthly minimum.

title: Yield Twins and Robotic Cells for Regional Beef Packers
one_liner: Start with 3D vision yield scoring on the fabrication line and grow into robotic trimming cells for independent packers.
customer: Independent regional beef packers processing under about 2,000 head a day.
problem: Record cattle prices and a 75-year-low herd squeeze packer margins, while skilled knife labor is scarce and immigration enforcement hits meatpacking labor hardest.
solution: A camera-based yield-and-trim-loss scoring system for cut optimization, then robotic primal trimming and portioning cells sold as a service.
why_now: Physical-AI and 3D-vision costs dropped in 2025-26, and thin packer margins make a 1% yield gain worth millions.
revenue_model: Software at $2-4k per month per line first, then per-head fees for robotic cells.
non_obvious_insight: With margins this thin, the software yield gain pays before any robot works, and the data it collects trains the robot.
first_30_days: Visit three independent packers, mount cameras on a fab line, and deliver a first weekly yield report as a paid pilot.

title: Mindbody Escape Hatch: Studio Migration Concierge
one_liner: A flat-fee service that moves a studio's members, class packs and payment tokens off Mindbody without losing revenue.
customer: Boutique studios, gyms, yoga and Pilates operators on Mindbody (about 40,000 businesses) paying $159-699 per month plus marketplace commissions.
problem: After the ClassPass/Mindbody/EGYM combination (a $7.5B deal completed in 2026), owners report about 23.5 percent effective marketplace commissions and a roughly $500 data-export fee on cancellation. Lock-in is not the software but the card-on-file payment tokens and member history, so owners fear migration will churn members.
solution: A fixed-fee migration ($1.5-3k): export clients, attendance, waivers, packs and memberships; execute PCI-compliant processor-to-processor token migration; map intro offers and unlimited plans; rebuild schedule widgets; run parallel billing checks; and message members by SMS. Target alternative platforms pay a bounty per migrated studio.
why_now: Consolidation gave studios a reason to re-evaluate, ClassPass is rolling out studio-friendly policies in response to complaints, and processors now support token migration.
revenue_model: $1.5-3k per migration plus $200-400 bounty per studio from the receiving software vendor and an optional $99 per month retention audit.
non_obvious_insight: The moat is edge-case knowledge (paused members, unlimited plans, refunds, tokens), not software, and rival vendors will pay you for customers because their own acquisition cost is high.
first_30_days: Offer five free migration audits in studio-owner communities, pick two target platforms, run three at-cost pilot migrations, and turn the playbook into a checklist and pricing page.

title: Signed Authority Certificates for Buying Agents
one_liner: Companies issue legally strong, machine-verifiable certificates saying which agent may order what, up to what amount, from whom, so suppliers can trust agent-placed orders.
customer: EU industrial distributors and wholesalers that receive purchase orders by email or EDI, and their larger business customers deploying procurement agents. Start with DACH and Benelux distributors.
problem: A supplier gets an order from 'Acme's purchasing agent' and has no way to know it may bind Acme to a EUR 50k purchase. AI makes fake purchase orders and business email compromise cheaper. Consumer-oriented agent-payment mandates (AP2, TAP, Verifiable Intent) do not cover B2B signing authority, and research notes from 2026 say agents do not map cleanly onto EU digital wallet categories.
solution: An authority registry and issuance service. A company's legal representative signs a delegation certificate (qualified electronic signature via eIDAS trust providers, EUDI wallet later) covering agent key, scope (categories or SKUs), per-order and monthly limits, validity and revocation. Suppliers verify by API in under 200 ms and see remaining limit. Integrate with ERP order intake and e-invoicing. The signed record is court-grade evidence in disputes.
why_now: EU member states must offer digital identity wallets by end-2026, financial institutions are expected to accept them by December 2027, and qualified signatures already carry the legal effect of handwritten ones. Agent mandate standards exist but are consumer-centric.
revenue_model: EUR 99-499/month per issuing company, EUR 0.05-0.20 per supplier verification, and enterprise licenses.
non_obvious_insight: Legal effect, not cryptography, is the scarce ingredient in B2B agent commerce. The EU uniquely has an instrument (the qualified signature) that turns a delegation into evidence courts accept, so build where the law already does the hard part.
first_30_days: Integrate with one qualified trust service provider for signing. Interview 20 distributors about agent-placed orders and PO fraud, pilot with 3 distributors and their top buyers on existing order intake, and collect letters of intent.

title: Muthoot-Style Gold Loans for America's Junk Drawers
one_liner: A mail-in, XRF-assayed loan against gold and jewelry at roughly 24-36% APR, versus 200%-plus at a typical US pawn shop, run through licensed pawn partners for people who need $300-$5,000 and have idle gold worth far more with gold trading around $4,100-$4,500 an ounce.
customer: Middle-income households aged 35-65 with jewelry and coins in a drawer and thin or damaged credit who need a few hundred to a few thousand dollars for a car repair, rent gap or tax bill. Small-business owners with a cash-flow gap are the second segment.
problem: Cash-for-gold buyers pay a fraction of melt value with no way to get the piece back. Pawn shops charge 10-25% a month. Payday and title lenders charge triple-digit APRs. The only cheap collateral-backed product is stigmatized, store-based and priced for rent rather than risk, so many people with real assets choose worse options or sell irreplaceable pieces at a loss.
solution: Mail an insured kit (or drop off at a partner pawn store). On receipt, run an XRF assay and weigh, then offer 70-75% of melt value within hours and pay by ACH. Redeem by paying principal plus interest, and the piece comes back insured. If the borrower does not repay, the gold is sold at melt with any surplus returned where state law requires. There is no collections calling and no credit reporting. Interest is about 2% a month falling for repeat borrowers. Hedge the collateral pool with gold futures. Launch through a licensed pawnbroker as lender of record, then license state by state.
why_now: Gold has traded roughly between $4,100 and $4,500 an ounce in September 2026, so a drawer of old 14k jewelry is worth several times what it was in 2022. Indian gold-loan lenders (Muthoot, Rupeek and others) have shown that 9-25% APR gold lending is profitable at scale, while US pawn remains a fragmented, store-based, high-rate market. Cheap XRF analyzers, insured shipping and instant ACH remove the storefront cost that justified those US rates.
revenue_model: Interest of 1.5-2.5% a month on outstanding loans, plus a small handling fee on loans under $500, plus surplus on forfeited gold sold above the loan amount. Funded by a private-credit warehouse line at low double-digit cost of capital. Because loans are 70-75% of a liquid commodity's melt value, credit losses are close to hedging and shipping costs.
non_obvious_insight: The 200%-plus APR of US pawn is not a price for risk, because collateral makes the loss very small. It is a price for store rent, low volume and stigma. Remove the storefront and the mass-market stigma (customers are gold owners with poor liquidity, not desperate borrowers) and you can undercut incumbents 5-8x on price and still earn better returns on capital than a bank.
first_30_days: Sign a licensed pawnbroker in Texas or Florida as lender of record so you inherit their license and compliance, including police reporting of transactions. Buy an XRF analyzer and a rated insured vault or use a custody partner. Raise about $250k to fund the first 50-100 loans. Buy search and social ads that intercept 'sell my gold' intent and publish the true APR up front. First loans should close within 4-6 weeks, and the pilot's default and hedging data becomes the pitch for a credit line.

title: Civil-Document Runners for Immigrant Families
one_liner: A vetted in-country network that retrieves, verifies and delivers birth, marriage, police and court records for consular and NVC cases, with chain-of-custody proof and no forged shortcuts.
customer: Immigration law firms and family-based petitioners (largely South Asian, Filipino, West African and Latin American communities) who pay $150-450 per document, plus rush fees and bundled certified translation and apostille.
problem: Applicants wait on USCIS, but the delays that lawyers dread most sit at the National Visa Center and consulate: 'documentarily qualified' rejections, requests for secondary evidence, and 221(g) refusals for a missing or irregular civil document. Every country issues records differently, and the State Department's reciprocity schedule is only a starting point. Families hire fixers or relatives, sometimes receive forged or improperly obtained records, and then face a permanent fraud bar (INA 212(a)(6)(C)). Lawyers keep private lists of trusted runners abroad. They cannot scale and are not available to families without counsel.
solution: A managed marketplace of vetted local partners (lawyers, licensed document agents, registry liaisons) in 8-10 high-volume corridors (India, Philippines, Mexico, Dominican Republic, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nigeria, Vietnam, El Salvador, Haiti). Each order starts with a pre-check against the consulate's actual document list, then a tracked retrieval from the issuing office with receipt and photo proof, an 'authenticity file' documenting exactly how the record was obtained, and delivery bundled with certified translation, apostille where applicable, and secondary-evidence packets when a record truly doesn't exist. Use online registries (India DigiLocker, Philippines PSA, Mexico's online actas) wherever possible so that most orders need little or no physical runner.
why_now: Consular processing has become slower and more discretionary, with more document-authenticity scrutiny, more public-charge-related evidence demands, and periodic pauses or holds by nationality. Errors that used to cost weeks now cost months. Many civil registries have digitized since 2020, so remote retrieval is now feasible for a meaningful share of documents, which makes a thin-margin logistics business viable for a small team.
revenue_model: Per-document fee ($150-450 depending on country and rush), roughly 40-50% gross margin after local partner costs, plus bundled translation and apostille, and a subscription tier for firms that order 20 or more documents a month.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody thinks of immigration as a logistics problem, so VCs fund form software while the real bottleneck is a birth certificate in a district registry that doesn't respond to email. The valuable asset is not software but a scorecard of which local partners and registry offices actually deliver on time and produce documents consulates accept. Reliability data by country and office can be built only by handling volume, and that is a moat lawyers already acknowledge privately.
first_30_days: Pick three corridors (Philippines, Mexico, India) where much of the retrieval can be done through official online portals plus one local partner. Sign 2 partners per corridor and pilot with 5 family-immigration firms at a flat price per document. Handle every order by hand, log time-to-delivery and rejection rates by office, and publish a country-by-country reliability guide to attract the next firms.
